passage: After the failed semester I made the list I now call my little list. Three lines only: go to every lecture, one hour of revision, five old questions. I wrote it on a sticky note and put it on my mirror. I had tried a big schedule before and it broke by the third day, so this time I kept it small on purpose. Some days I did only the first line and felt fine. My flatmate Shankar asked to look at it once, and I felt a little shy, but I showed him. By week three the ticks made a row, and I did not want to break it. On one awful day, when the lab report ate everything, I still got two of three. — Sangeeta

Student mentor's note, Ayesha (second year), week 4 of the new term.
After failing two courses last semester, Ayesha came to me wanting a "total transformation". We agreed on something much smaller: a daily checklist of only three lines. Attend every class. Revise one hour. Solve five past questions. Nothing else counted.
She keeps it on an index card in her phone cover. Her friend Mahima checks in with her at dinner: "How many ticks?"
This week she told me about Tuesday. She'd slept badly, felt low, and didn't want to leave her bed. She almost skipped everything. Then she looked at the card and thought: three things, I can do three things. She went to class, did forty minutes of revision instead of an hour, and five questions. "Not perfect, but not zero," she said.
Next step: keep the list at three until mid-terms. Only then consider adding a fourth.

qa.q: Where does Ayesha keep the checklist?
qa.a: On an index card in her phone cover.

qa.q: How was Ayesha feeling on Tuesday?
qa.a: Ayesha felt low and tired after sleeping badly, and didn't want to leave her bed.

qa.q: What else could help Ayesha keep the list going?
qa.a: Ayesha could note her ticks each week and share them with Mahima or the mentor, so progress stays visible even in messy weeks.
Mahima asks about the ticks at dinner, giving friendly daily accountability without pressure.

grounding: Shows a student rebuilding routine with a small daily checklist of class, one hour of revision and five past questions, small enough to keep on a bad day.

passage:
Friday
Day 12 of the list. Still three lines on the sticky note above my desk:
1. Go to every class.
2. One hour of revision.
3. Five past-paper questions.
That's it. After last semester's two failures, I wanted to do everything: eight-hour days, colour-coded notes. Darshan said, "You'll quit in a week. Make it so small you can't fail it." Annoying, but he's usually right.
Today was bad. Mum called, worried about fees, I slept through breakfast, and I cried in the washroom before the 10 am lecture. I still went. Did the hour in the library, badly. Did five questions, got two wrong.
Three ticks. On a day like this, three ticks.
I think that's the point of a small list. A bad day can't knock it over.
Gurleen

qa.q: How many past-paper questions are on the list?

qa.a: Gurleen felt upset and drained, crying before the lecture after a stressful call and a missed breakfast.

qa.q: What else could Gurleen do on the hardest days?
qa.a: Gurleen could also reach out to Darshan or the campus counsellor when a day feels that heavy, so the list isn't the only support.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel reading today's entry?
qa.a: Darshan would likely feel proud and relieved that the small list held on a hard day, as he had hoped.

grounding: Illustrates a student keeping a tiny daily checklist after a failed semester and managing all three items even on a bad day.
